vignette:
Michael, a 47-year-old bus driver, had been driving the same night route for over a decade when the incident occurred. It was just past midnight, and he had pulled over to check a flickering taillight. Within minutes, a police cruiser was behind him, lights flashing. What followed was a blur of shouting, the cold press of asphalt against his cheek, and hands pulling his arms behind his back. He was handcuffed, searched, and left kneeling on the roadside while officers ran his information. They found nothing-the taillight was a faulty bulb-but the apology never came. What stayed was the image of a boot inches from his face and the memory of his own voice cracking as he tried to explain he was just a bus driver, not a threat.

In the weeks that followed, that memory kept arriving without warning. It would flash behind his eyes mid-turn, just as a passenger asked for a stop, or while he waited at a red light. The worst was when a police car appeared in his rearview mirror. His hands would lock on the wheel, his throat tightened, and he'd start scanning for an exit before remembering he hadn't done anything wrong. Talking about the event was unbearable. When a coworker once asked what happened, Michael's response was to press his palms flat over his eyes, blocking out the room, until the question dissolved into silence. He began covering his face whenever tension rose-during minor confrontations, when a passenger complained, even when the news showed a police report. It was the only thing that made the images stop for a moment.

At home, Michael turned the television up so loud his neighbor complained. He could not stand the quiet; silence let the memory breathe. He filled his apartment with noise-blaring music, action movies, anything to drown the internal replay. He stopped answering calls from old friends. The few people he'd once had beers with after shifts gradually stopped trying. He told himself it was safer this way. People couldn't be trusted. He had learned that lesson. The world, he was certain, was a place where you followed every rule and still ended up on your knees. That belief became a lens through which he saw every stranger, every approaching figure, every unexpected knock.

His temper frayed. On the bus, a passenger taking too long to tap their card would earn a sharp word. Another driver cutting him off would trigger a string of curses through the closed window. He was aware of the anger-felt it burning in his chest-but it seemed to come from somewhere outside himself, like a reflex he could not stop. Concentration became a struggle. He would miss his stop markers, drive past his depot, or find himself staring at the dashboard clock with no memory of the last ten minutes. At night, he checked the front door three, four times before bed, then the windows, then back to the door. He knew it didn't make sense-he lived on the third floor-but the ritual was the only thing that quieted the sense that something was about to break in.

The sense of belonging he'd once felt in his neighborhood evaporated. He no longer acknowledged the regulars at the corner store. He crossed the street when he saw a police cruiser. The community he'd been part of-the block parties, the morning nods at the coffee shop-felt like a ghost world he was no longer permitted to enter. He had lost his connection to it, though he could not say exactly when the door closed.

Last week, a police car passed him on the route. Michael's hands flew to his face as he drove, and when he lowered them, he had drifted into the next lane. A pedestrian had to jump back. His supervisor called him in the next day. Michael sat in the office, covering his face again, and said nothing. That night, he searched online for help. What frightened him most was not the near-miss-it was the certainty that if he kept going this way, he would lose his job, and without the bus, he would dissolve into the silence he was trying so hard to outrun. He wanted someone to tell him it could be different, even if he did not believe it yet.
